independence_rule: Facts were established from the local Book V chapter text before comparison with production JSON or the Book V production manifest. Canonical IDs are normalization labels only; source-era names, aliases, reported outcomes, coercion, intended destinations and actual outcomes remain distinct.

chapters.title: The Abduction
historical_context: Fugen and Monju imagery used as narrative comparison

facts.description: Musashi, Otsū and Jōtarō continue east after Magome, with Musashi deliberately walking ahead while Otsū and Jōtarō follow with the cow.
Otsū uses Karasumaru Mitsuhiro's letter of introduction to pass the Fukushima barrier with Jōtarō.
Jōtarō recognizes Matahachi near Fukushima and the road party is brought into direct contact with him.
Matahachi seizes Otsū and refuses to accept the end of their former engagement.
Jōtarō attacks Matahachi with his wooden sword in defense of Otsū.
Matahachi overpowers Jōtarō and throws him down into the stream/bamboo below the road.
Matahachi takes control of the cow and carries Otsū away by force.
Musashi, waiting farther along the road, realizes Otsū and Jōtarō are overdue and turns back to find them.
Witnesses confirm that a young woman was taken away and Musashi follows the side-road clues from the barrier.
Finding Otsū's cow at Gonnosuke's farm, Musashi wrongly concludes that Gonnosuke abducted Otsū and Jōtarō.
Musashi and Musō Gonnosuke fight with sword and staff because of the misunderstanding; Musashi gains control of Gonnosuke without killing him.
Gonnosuke's mother threatens Musashi with a lance, forcing the parties to stop and clarify what happened.
Gonnosuke explains that he merely found the abandoned cow near Nobu Pond; he and his mother become allies in the search.
Musashi and Gonnosuke question households around Nobu Pond for news of Otsū and Jōtarō.
A local woman reports seeing a muddy boy with a long wooden sword running toward Yabuhara and says he was directed to Daizō, the wealthy herb dealer of Narai.
Musashi accepts Narai as the strongest lead and crosses Nobu Pond with Gonnosuke before continuing the search.

chapters.title: Poisonous Fangs
functional_actors: farmer/grain carrier whose horse is taken

facts.description: Matahachi hides the bound Otsū at a tiny shrine when he sees light and movement on Nobu Pond.
Matahachi binds, drags and lashes Otsū while demanding that she submit to him.
Otsū rejects Matahachi and states that her love for Musashi will not change.
Matahachi bites through Otsū's sleeve into her upper arm until she loses consciousness, describing the wound as a permanent mark of his ownership.
Matahachi coerces a passing farmer and requisitions his horse to continue transporting Otsū.
To avoid pursuit on the Nakasendō, Matahachi chooses a clandestine route toward Ina and Kōshū by way of Ubagami and Gombei Pass.
At dawn Otsū persuades Matahachi to release the farmer and horse rather than continue holding an uninvolved man in the abduction.
Gonnosuke interprets the earlier defeat as proof that he should abandon martial training.
Gonnosuke's mother refuses to let him surrender his calling and urges him to challenge Musashi again.
Musashi overhears the family discussion and leaves without confrontation, unwilling to crush Gonnosuke while he is demoralized.
At Narai, Musashi learns that Daizō and Jōtarō left hours earlier, with uncertain plans involving Zenkōji/Echigo and ultimately Edo.
Musashi leaves a sign/trace for Daizō and Jōtarō and waits around Shiojiri Pass and Sengen Shrine.
The sight of Mount Fuji humbles Musashi and reframes his ideas of human greatness and discipline.
Gonnosuke and his mother catch up; formal introductions precede a second sword-versus-staff bout.
Gonnosuke's staff reaches Musashi's chest while Musashi deliberately strikes with the ridge rather than the cutting edge of his sword.
Musashi refuses a simplistic winner/loser reading, acknowledges Gonnosuke's mark on him and recognizes the mother's low-hip insight as genuine martial instruction.
Musashi continues through Inojigahara toward Kamisuwa while an unidentified samurai follows him.

chapters.title: A One-Night Love Affair
historical_context: political future of Edo and the great houses

facts.description: Pain from Gonnosuke's strike leads Musashi to suspend the search temporarily and recuperate at the Shimosuwa hot springs.
Ishimoda Geki, a retainer of Date Masamune, reveals that he has deliberately sought Musashi after hearing of his reputation.
Geki befriends and hosts Musashi, expressing unusually open admiration for him.
Geki describes Date Masamune's ambitions and frames military ability as service to a broader political order rather than private fame.
Geki asks Musashi for whose sake he is perfecting swordsmanship, forcing him to confront the purpose behind his training.
Geki invites Musashi to Sendai and offers to recommend him to Date Masamune.
Musashi concludes that technique and defeating opponents cannot be the final goal; he seeks an all-embracing Way of the Sword that answers how to live.
Musashi refuses to abandon the search for Otsū and Jōtarō to travel to Edo with Geki; Geki departs separately.
Musashi hires Suwa laborers to search for Daizō and Jōtarō; most take the money without doing the promised work.
One honest laborer actually searches and reports that Daizō and Jōtarō headed toward Wada Pass.
Musashi rewards the honest laborer with his remaining ordinary cash and continues the route nearly penniless.
At a roadside teahouse Musashi discovers a money pouch and letter secretly planted by Geki as travel expenses.
Musashi recognizes the unsolicited money as a possible political obligation binding him toward Date service and resists using it.
One of the teahouse men follows Musashi, pretends to return a dropped silver piece and lures him onto a side trail under the pretext of lodging.
The guide attempts to drop a log bridge beneath Musashi; Musashi anticipates the move and kills him.
A concealed musketeer fires and misses while additional attackers close in, carrying the ambush into the next chapter.
Musashi survives the firearm ambush, kills the musketeer and drives the remaining attacker uphill.
The bandit chief is revealed to be Gion Tōji, formerly of the Yoshioka circle.
The woman at the bandit refuge recognizes Musashi as Takezō and is revealed as Okō.
The three temporarily set aside hostility, eat together and exchange news about their paths since Kyoto.
Musashi tells Okō that Akemi and Matahachi had planned to go east and that Akemi had fled with money.
Behind Musashi's back, Tōji resolves to kill him and summons more than twenty bandits, linking revenge and criminal gain.
The bandits place Musashi in a detachable rear room above the ravine and pull away its supports so it crashes down the slope.
Musashi anticipates the trap and escapes rather than falling with the room.
The refuge is left burning and Okō is tied to a tree while the gang searches unsuccessfully for Musashi; the fire functions as destruction of the bandit base rather than a simple duel outcome.

chapters.title: Playing with Fire
functional_actors: unnamed rōnin who attacks Jōtarō and carries Akemi away

facts.description: Shōji Jinnai leads a large Sumiya party of prostitutes and staff east toward the new Yoshiwara; Akemi is traveling with them but has not yet irrevocably committed herself.
Kojirō meets Jinnai at Kobotoke Pass; Akemi hides to avoid being seen by Kojirō and later rejoins the caravan.
Daizō's party and the Sumiya caravan lodge at the same Hachiōji inn.
Jōtarō and Akemi recognize one another and leave the crowded inn to talk privately.
Akemi learns from Jōtarō that Otsū is traveling with Musashi and that Jōtarō believes Musashi loves Otsū; jealousy overwhelms her.
Akemi drinks heavily, speaks of death and moves toward the moat while Jōtarō tries to restrain and protect her.
An unnamed rōnin intervenes, violently throws/knocks Jōtarō unconscious and carries Akemi away.
Akemi is later found disheveled on hay with her kimono open and obi removed; the scene and observers strongly imply sexual assault, although the narration does not explicitly state the act.
Jōtarō recovers and returns toward Daizō rather than continuing the confrontation.
Jōtarō sees a disguised man descend the old fortress cliff and secretly follows him after recognizing Daizō.
At the Head-burying Mound Daizō buries a very large cache of gold ingots and coins and carefully disguises the site while Jōtarō watches unseen.
Jōtarō returns to the inn before Daizō and pretends not to know what happened.
On the road toward Edo Jōtarō asks to leave Daizō and resume searching for Musashi.
Daizō reveals that he knows Jōtarō witnessed the buried gold.
Daizō forces Jōtarō to choose between becoming his adopted son and being killed, while promising to make him a samurai.
When Jōtarō calls him a thief, Daizō denies being a common criminal and compares his ambitions to rulers who seize whole countries.
Daizō declares Jōtarō his son and explicitly threatens to kill him if he reveals the gold cache.

chapters.title: The Pioneers
historical_context: Tokugawa Ieyasu and the rapid construction of Edo
early Edo land speculation and neighborhood self-policing

facts.description: After nearly two months of slow travel from Kyoto, Osugi arrives in rapidly expanding Edo and initially despises the muddy construction city.
Osugi quarrels with plasterers after being splattered with clay and demonstrates that her old combative temperament is intact.
A pickpocket steals Osugi's purse while her kimono is drying near a public bath.
Osugi catches the thief and slashes his ankle even after being kicked hard enough to collapse.
Hangawara Yajibei catches the thief, restores Osugi's property and takes charge of her safety.
Yajibei orders the thief publicly tied to a stake for seven days while still being given enough food to survive.
Yajibei has Osugi carried through Nihombashi to his Bakurōchō household rather than leave the injured old woman alone.
A year and a half after arrival, Osugi still lives under Yajibei's protection and his men remain under orders to report any trace of Musashi.
Yajibei takes Osugi, Jūrō and Koroku by boat to Sensōji on the anniversary of his mother's death.
Before Kanzeon, Osugi explicitly prays both to strike Musashi down and to have Matahachi made a good son.
A donor plaque records that Daizō of Narai gave ten gold coins to Sensōji, providing evidence that his path reached Edo.
Kojirō defeats four Obata-school opponents on the Sumida bank and kills the last wounded man when he attempts to continue the fight.
Osugi recognizes Kojirō after the slaughter and calls him back.
Osugi introduces Kojirō to Yajibei, joining two previously separate sources of support for her vendetta.

chapters.title: Shavings
historical_context: Yagyū and other Edo sword schools used as comparison

facts.description: Kojirō offers continued help in Osugi's search for Musashi and Yajibei treats him as a powerful ally.
Yajibei asks Kojirō to train his forty-to-fifty henchmen and Kojirō agrees to conduct rough sessions three times a month.
Kojirō's training rapidly causes serious injuries, permanent disability and at least one trainee's death; he shows no remorse.
After training, Kojirō has Jūrō and Koroku guide him to the new Yoshiwara pleasure quarter.
Akemi is now working at the Sumiya under the professional name Hanagiri.
Akemi recognizes Kojirō at the Sumiya and hides in the construction shavings rather than meet him.
After drinking sake, Akemi slips out of the Sumiya and runs away from Jinnai's establishment into Edo.

chapters.title: The Owl
functional_actors: Obata Academy students and wounded survivors
physical_locations: Obata Academy at Hirakawa Tenjin Shrine

facts.description: About ten Obata students ambush Kojirō after his Yoshiwara outing in revenge for the Sumida deaths.
Kojirō defeats the attackers; five ultimately die while surviving students return badly wounded.
Hōjō Shinzō condemns the students for repeatedly challenging a swordsman they do not understand and argues that revenge over insults is strategically meaningless.
Shinzō continues nursing the gravely ill Kagenori while assuming much of the academy's teaching burden.
Kojirō secretly follows the survivors home, appears at the academy while they plan another challenge and publicly humiliates them without needing another battle.
Deaths and humiliation deepen the academy's decline while Kagenori remains near death and largely shielded from the details.
After learning that Kagenori's son Yogorō is returning, Shinzō leaves a farewell letter and departs alone to seek Kojirō's head.

chapters.title: A Plate of Loaches
historical_context: Misawa family service to the Mogami clan
Taira no Masakado and the Shimōsa plain

facts.description: After returning Geki's money in Sendai and continuing ascetic travel, Musashi reaches Hōtengahara about a year and a half later.
Musashi meets a twelve-year-old boy still called Sannosuke while the boy catches loaches and accepts his offer of shelter.
Sannosuke reveals that his father died that morning and that he planned to cut the corpse in half because he could not carry it intact to the burial ground.
Musashi contributes strength rather than money and helps Sannosuke transport and bury his father intact.
Sannosuke explains that his grandfather Misawa Iori abandoned samurai status rather than serve a second lord, while his father lived as the farmer San'emon.
Now orphaned, Sannosuke asks to travel with Musashi as groom and ultimately become a samurai.
Musashi tests the boy harshly in combat and repeatedly overpowers him, but Sannosuke refuses to concede while alive.
Impressed by the boy's tenacity, Musashi accepts Sannosuke as his pupil.
Musashi renames Sannosuke 'Iori' after his samurai grandfather, giving the boy a source of identity and aspiration before formal adulthood.
Musashi burns the old family shack so it cannot become a bandit refuge and to mark the end of Iori's inherited peasant household.
Instead of resuming wandering, Musashi decides that they will build a new house and use Hōtengahara itself as their training ground.
Musashi lays aside the sword for sustained work with axe and hoe, treating cultivation and self-support as part of martial discipline.
Musashi begins teaching Iori work, reading, writing and conduct while also learning from the boy's practical weather sense and resilience.
Repeated storms and floods destroy the fields and dikes despite enormous labor, confronting Musashi with a problem brute will cannot solve.
Musashi realizes he has been forcing water and soil into an imported rectangular-field design rather than understanding the terrain's own nature.
He changes strategy to work with the flow of water and contours of the land, writing that one must not oppose the way of the universe without first understanding it.
Nagaoka Sado, senior Hosokawa retainer, visits Tokuganji privately and notices Iori, not yet knowing his teacher.
On the way home Iori discovers forty-to-fifty mountain bandits gathering before a raid and tries to seek help.
Bandit guards capture and bind Iori to a bridge post; a mortally wounded villager frees him before dying.
Iori reaches Musashi and reports the raid, asking him to save the village.
Musashi attacks the bandits transporting captive women, kills armed raiders and begins freeing the victims.
Musashi organizes the villagers into concealed groups, teaches them to attack isolated returning raiders and converts numerical superiority into coordinated defense.
Musashi and the villagers destroy most of the raiding force; Musashi then leads the counterattack into the village and kills the bandit chief.
After victory Musashi warns the villagers not to become proud of violence and tells them their proper business remains agriculture.
Sado investigates the aftermath, learns that Miyamoto Musashi organized the defense and becomes interested in meeting him.
Musashi leaves the village the maxim that the plow is the sword and the sword the plow, linking defense, work and continuity across generations.
Iwama Kakubei asks Sado to recommend his relative-by-marriage and houseguest Sasaki Kojirō to Hosokawa Tadatoshi.
Tadatoshi agrees to examine Kojirō but reminds Sado that he also wants to see the rōnin Musashi whom Sado had previously praised.
Recognizing that he delayed too long, Sado rides immediately to Hōtengahara to find Musashi.
Sado finds the former wasteland transformed into productive rice, hemp and barley fields through Musashi and Iori's work with the villagers.
Villagers report that Musashi taught them self-reliance, solidarity and labor for the benefit of future generations rather than dependence on him.
The morning after the community celebration, Musashi and Iori leave Hōtengahara without ceremony so the village will continue independently.
The villagers place Musashi's carved Kannon in a small shrine and honor it on the way to and from the fields.
Sado realizes that his delay has cost him the chance to meet and potentially recruit Musashi for Tadatoshi.
Musashi and Iori pass the newly strict east-bank barrier and enter Edo after Musashi claims Yagyū Munenori as his local connection.
Musashi reflects that it is too late to test Sekishūsai but still longs to test himself against Munenori.
After the ferry, Iori rudely claims his dropped pouch; Jūrō confronts him until Musashi intervenes and learns Jūrō belongs to Hangawara's group.
Musashi uses the incident to teach Iori that etiquette restrains people's bad side and is essential in crowded civic life.
Musashi unexpectedly meets Kimura Sukekurō in the Bakurōchō horse market; their former near-hostility has become cordial.
Sukekurō invites Musashi to the Yagyū household and cryptically says they possess a beautiful treasure belonging to him.
When horse trader Kumagorō threatens him over noise complaints, Musashi silently plucks live flies from his soba with chopsticks, causing the traders to retreat.
After receiving Munenori's invitation through Sukekurō, Musashi replies that as a warrior his only purpose in visiting is to have a bout.
Musashi sends Iori at night to deliver the challenge reply to the Yagyū household.

chapters.title: The Soul Polisher
physical_locations: Zushino Kōsuke's Bakurōchō shop and house

facts.description: Kōsuke initially refuses to polish Musashi's nicked sword because Musashi asks only for a sharper cutting weapon.
Kōsuke explains Kōetsu's teaching that the craftsman's real work is polishing the samurai's soul and that a sword exists to preserve integrity and order, not delight in killing.
Musashi accepts the criticism and recognizes that he has not adequately considered the moral spirit of the sword he carries.
Kōsuke offers Musashi a prized sword in exchange for a carved Kannon rather than ordinary payment and invites him to stay at the house.
Kōsuke shows a very long rusted sword; Musashi recognizes it as Kojirō's Drying Pole.
Kōsuke explains that Iwama Kakubei delivered the Drying Pole on behalf of his houseguest and asked for polishing and refitting.
Returning late to the inn, Musashi finds Iori still absent from the Yagyū errand and waits outside in growing concern.

chapters.title: The Fox
historical_context: Iigura shrine and old Kamakura routes

facts.description: Iori reaches Kobikichō only to learn the Yagyū residence is actually at Higakubo; he sleeps at a storehouse and resumes the errand the next day.
Iori repeatedly loses time sightseeing through Edo's construction districts while trying to reach Higakubo.
Iori cuts a fox in Azabu and becomes convinced the animal is bewitching him and causing his confusion.
Iori sees a veiled flute-playing Otsū and the slightly limping Hyōgo and, in his fear, mistakes both for fox spirits in human form.
The narration reveals that Otsū endured years traveling under Matahachi's control without yielding sexually, until Sukekurō encountered them and took her into Yagyū protection.
In the recalled rescue, Sukekurō tells Matahachi to bring any objection to Higakubo, and Matahachi is powerless to stop Otsū leaving with the Yagyū party.
Otsū and Hyōgo have formed a close but carefully bounded friendship during her stay with the Yagyū household.

chapters.title: An Urgent Letter
historical_context: Tokugawa Hidetada and Munenori's role as shogunal instructor

facts.description: Munenori worries that keeping a young woman indefinitely in a household full of unmarried samurai may create scandal or rash behavior and asks Hyōgo/Sukekurō to find a humane solution.
A fast courier from Koyagyū reports that Sekishūsai has suffered a much worse spell and may be dying.
Unable to abandon his Edo duties, Munenori sends Hyōgo to Koyagyū to care for Sekishūsai in his place.
Otsū asks to accompany Hyōgo so she can repay Sekishūsai's past kindness by helping at his bedside; Munenori permits and supports her departure.
On Dōgen Slope the departing Otsū and Hyōgo encounter exhausted Iori, who still thinks they may be foxes.
After frightening Iori out of his fox delusion, Hyōgo gives him accurate directions to the nearby Yagyū house.
Iori carries Musashi's letter past the woman Musashi has long sought, while neither Iori nor Otsū realizes the other's connection to Musashi.

chapters.title: Filial Piety
historical_context: Sutra on the Great Love of Parents

facts.description: Osugi copies the Sutra on the Great Love of Parents and vows to produce a thousand copies, explicitly linking the vow to her grief over Matahachi's lack of filial conduct.
Jūrō tells Osugi that he encountered Musashi at the Sumida ferry and followed him to lodging in Bakurōchō.
Jūrō has a man keep watch and subsequently learns Musashi moved from the inn to Zushino Kōsuke's house.
Unwilling to wait for Yajibei, Osugi sets out to consult Kojirō at Iwama Kakubei's house about attacking Musashi.
Jūrō and the Hangawara men initially mock Osugi's sutra but become emotionally overwhelmed by its description of parental sacrifice and filial neglect.
Kojirō walks into the Hangawara room at the end of the reading, just as the men are unusually vulnerable and reflective.
Kojirō proposes acting as Osugi's second and devises a plan to lure Musashi outside, draw first and give Osugi the opening to strike.
Osugi prepares as if for her own death, wearing a shrine-stamped burial robe and carrying letters, a filial-piety sutra and her family short sword.
Kojirō visits Kōsuke under the pretext of collecting the Drying Pole and asks to see Musashi so the ambush can proceed.
Before Kojirō can execute his plan, Hōjō Shinzō attacks the waiting group, mortally wounding Jūrō and Koroku and knocking Osugi into a ditch.
Kojirō initially assumes Musashi struck his companions but the dying Koroku makes clear the attacker was someone else.
Shinzō openly identifies himself and attacks Kojirō for insulting Kagenori and killing Obata students.
Kojirō's rapid draw slices flesh from Shinzō's neck and exposes the carotid without quite killing him.
Kōsuke reaches the collapsing Shinzō, calls for help and brings him into the house for emergency treatment.

chapters.title: A Block of Wood
functional_actors: doctor and neighbors who help Shinzō
historical_context: Prince Shōtoku-era temple wood used for the carving

facts.description: Musashi works almost continuously on the promised Kannon, repeatedly reducing an ancient block because he cannot make the inner image emerge faithfully.
Examining Shinzō's neck wound, Musashi recognizes the shape as consistent with Kojirō's swallow-flight stroke.
After roughly forty-eight hours of effort the block is nearly exhausted; Musashi declares the carving a failure and turns to meditation rather than forcing the form.
Iori finally returns after the three-day errand and apologizes for the delay.
Sukekurō's reply explains that Munenori cannot accept a formal bout because of his position as shogunal tutor.
The letter suggests Hyōgo as the proper Yagyū opponent but says he has just left for Yamato because Sekishūsai is gravely ill.
Iori blames his long delay on a fox; Musashi reframes the punishment as Iori's own invisible conscience reacting to his choices.
Musashi leaves for the Obata academy to report Shinzō's condition on Kōsuke's behalf.

chapters.title: The Deserted Prophet
historical_context: Kōshū military science and transition from conquest to governance

facts.description: Musashi informs Kagenori's son Yogorō that Shinzō has been badly wounded and should remain at Kōsuke's house until stronger.
Musashi urges Yogorō not to continue the feud, describing Kojirō as exceptionally dangerous and the original grievance as too trivial to justify further disaster.
The academy is nearly deserted because of Kagenori's illness, Kojirō's humiliations and students transferring elsewhere.
From his sickroom Kagenori notices Musashi's effortless situational awareness as he enters and decides he wants to meet him.
Kagenori tells Yogorō that his military science is now aimed at peace and stability and that he needs the right mature man to receive it because Yogorō is not ready.
Yogorō searches for Musashi but fails to bring him back before the opportunity closes.
Hosokawa retainer Nakatogawa Handayū tells Yogorō that news of Shinzō's defeat by Kojirō is already circulating at the Hosokawa house, hardening Yogorō's resolve.
Iori discovers another man spying on Kōsuke's house, confirming persistent Hangawara surveillance around the recovering Shinzō.
Shinzō decides he has recovered enough to leave despite Kōsuke's warning that Hangawara men are waiting outside.
Musashi arrives as Shinzō is leaving and insists on escorting him, ultimately placing the weakened man in a palanquin.
Hangawara men led by Nembutsu Tazaemon surround Musashi and Shinzō, demanding Shinzō for killing Jūrō and Koroku.
Musashi argues that Shinzō's revenge against Kojirō's associates belongs to warrior custom and tries to move the dispute away from gang retaliation and street bloodshed.
When Tazaemon attacks, Musashi throws him into the moat, picks up Shinzō and runs rather than slaughter the gang.
Musashi explicitly teaches Shinzō that there are circumstances in which running away is wiser and more satisfying than answering insults with lethal force.
Edo gossip interprets Musashi's restraint as cowardice, branding him a fraud and retroactively belittling his Yoshioka victories.
Signs appear throughout Edo calling Musashi a coward and challenging him to face the Hon'iden dowager and the Hangawara Association.
